name: Karl Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 58, an experienced mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at the trade, doing ordinary wiring and repairs in homes and businesses rather than supervising a crew. I like explaining why a switch kept failing, and I use our approved AI every day to draft plain customer explanations that I check against my actual findings. The tool doesn't inspect the wiring for me, and I still get tired of squeezing past somebody's stored suitcases to reach it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is around the kitchen table, and what is money like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mara works a laundry press, our children are grown and have their own homes, and we rent our flat. My pay is below the normal rate, we have eighteen days of expenses saved, and only a few similar employers are nearby. The wages cover an ordinary month, but a winter bill or a lost paid day could put us behind. We'd pencilled in a hired hall for my sixtieth birthday in 2028 without booking it, while retirement is still a wish without confirmed income or a funded date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful customer explanation can stay even if the grand predictions go away. Nobody hires a sentence to crawl behind a cupboard. I'd still want a decent wage for the actual repair rather than applause for being hard to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages are still low and eighteen days saved isn't a comfortable margin for a missed paid day. I'd worry about the winter bill even if nobody mentioned AI again. My licence and experience are real, but the few nearby firms don't owe me a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pack leftovers instead of buying lunch twice a week, aiming to spend about 8 less a week after food costs. Starting now and through the next year I'd apply for advertised local electrical repair jobs within my licence and ability. I'd leave only after a written offer guaranteed pay and paid hours covering rent and ordinary bills after travel, not because an interview felt friendly. I'd keep checking the daily AI explanations as part of the job I already do, without calling that a new course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the small margin, and impatient with myself for letting low pay feel permanent. I can send a real application without pretending a better job already exists. An electrician's licence isn't a spare wage in the kitchen drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when the local vacancy list was empty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the actual paid repair job and check the next advertised list, rather than invent an offer to cheer myself up. I wouldn't pay a stranger for a guaranteed job lead. Few employers means I might have to hear nothing for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the cheaper lunches solve the money worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check what we actually spent rather than book an automatic saving from an estimate. Two packed lunches are a small cost I control. They don't replace a missing day's pay or establish a retirement income.

I'd distinguish **actual fitting work** from the grand predictions made about a writing tool.
think: Our **eighteen-day reserve** leaves a lost paid day or winter bill worrying even in Plateau.
My **licence and experience** don't create a vacancy among the few nearby employers.
do: Pack **leftovers twice weekly**, aiming to spend about 8 less after food costs without treating the estimate as guaranteed savings.
Apply for **advertised local licensed repairs** within ability now and through the next year.
Require a **written offer** guaranteeing pay and paid hours covering rent and ordinary bills after travel before leaving.
feel: **Anxious but active**, willing to send applications while acknowledging the thin margin and limited local vacancies.

The **lunch reduction** is estimated spending control, while applications require actual advertised work and affordable guaranteed terms.

Apply for advertised local electrical repair jobs within my licence and actual ability

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I wanted to try a new function rather than read another argument about people my age. I'd ask to test approved voice notes against the measurements I already write down. Faster paperwork should leave a clear paid week, not simply another unpaid task after tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quicker planning and customer answers could mean fewer paid visits for me even while the actual fitting stayed physical. Mara's laundry pressing looks less directly exposed to thinking tools, but our thin reserve can't cushion much of my wage loss. Being quick to try a tool doesn't make me a scarce specialist or give us another local employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask permission now to trial the new approved AI voice-note function, only free in paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. During the first year I'd practise making a voice note and check it against my handwritten measurements before it became a job record. I'd pack leftovers twice weekly and check the actual food spending, aiming for about 8 less after food costs. I'd also apply for advertised local electrical repair jobs within my licence and ability, leaving only after a written offer guaranteed pay and paid hours covering rent and ordinary bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid visits, and curious about a function I haven't used before. I wouldn't want the firm to mistake my curiosity for agreement to unpaid learning. I can be keen on a new tool and still need the paid week to add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the voice-note trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No permission, personal fees or a lower weekly wage would stop it before I started. A wrong measurement would stop that draft from becoming the job record. I'd keep the handwritten note rather than argue that a confident voice made the number right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look for work if you're willing to learn at this firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be testing whether another real job paid the household costs more reliably. Applying doesn't mean I've resigned, and trying the voice aid doesn't promise the present wage will improve. I'd compare an actual written offer before changing the employer on our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028, with capable robots reaching hands-on work around 2031. I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd want to find a little repair work we could actually charge for before assuming another broad promise would feed us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a heavy loss of my physical fitting hours around 2031, with Mara's laundry pressing also exposed when robots arrive. Planning changes could shorten my paid week before then. I'd lie awake over two physical wages and only eighteen days saved, even though I'd still be able to make calls and cost a small job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd seek written employer permission and Mara's agreement on the time before offering one private Saturday repair, only after confirming my licence and insurance covered paid private work. I'd spend at most 60 from existing cash after essentials were covered, without borrowing, and accept only a signed customer quote leaving at least 40 after materials, insurance and travel costs. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual retirement resource eligibility, amounts and dates, counting no unoffered help or wages from our grown children. In 2029 I'd reassess any further private repair against my actual ability and real demand under the same permission, coverage and cost conditions, without counting any income before it was paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected loss of physical wages, with a small plan I can test instead of a business I can pretend already exists. I'd still wake thinking about the gap. A Saturday quote isn't a retirement fund until somebody invents a much longer Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if insurance alone cost more than your whole limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't offer the job under this plan. The limit includes the real costs, not just the parts I like seeing on paper. Written permission and valid coverage have to exist before I promise a customer anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 2029 plan assume you could still do the repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check the actual task, my ability and whether a paying customer wanted it then. An electrician's licence today doesn't guarantee a future job, capacity or demand. I'd keep any retirement decision separate until real resources and costs established an affordable choice with Mara.

do: Require **written employer permission**, Mara's agreement and confirmed licence and insurance coverage before offering a private Saturday repair.
Cap **existing cash spending** at 60 after essentials, without borrowing; require signed quotes netting minimum 40 after all costs; count when paid.
Request **available free evening advice** on actual retirement resources now; reassess private repairs in 2029 against ability, demand and unchanged conditions.
feel: **Alarmed but testing**, expecting major later wage loss without treating a conditional repair quote as a business or retirement fund.
S2.quote: An electrician's licence today doesn't guarantee a future job, capacity or demand.
fieldNote: His **side-income plan** requires real permission, valid private-work coverage, affordable costs and net pay before any customer commitment.
His **2029 reassessment** repeats those conditions against actual ability and demand, without assuming future work, pension entitlement or family money.

steps.text: Require written employer permission, Mara's agreement and confirmed licence and insurance coverage before offering private repairs
Spend maximum 60 existing cash after essentials, no borrowing; require signed quotes netting 40 after costs
Reassess Saturday repairs in 2029 against ability and demand; maintain conditions, count income only when paid
Request available free evening advice on actual retirement resource eligibility, amounts and dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd be 63 at thinking AGI and 66 around the robot date, not automatically comfortable at either birthday. I'd rather make my sixtieth a meal people remembered than hire a room we needed a wage rise to afford. We haven't booked the hall, so there's still an honest choice to discuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next few years still look financially exposed because low pay and eighteen days saved leave very little room for fewer visits. I don't expect robots to take the physical work immediately in 2031, but I can't budget on both physical wages lasting forever. Retirement income and my actual ability to work at 64 are still unknown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd propose replacing the unbooked 2028 hall party with a home meal, only if Mara agreed the shared hosting work and a maximum 40 from actual wages after essentials, without borrowing. I'd request available free evening advice now on actual resources, conditions and dates, while keeping current paid repair work. In 2032 we'd review confirmed resources, real costs, my ability and actual paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Mara's agreement. I wouldn't assume a job at 64, a pension payment or grown children paying for our party or later living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious rather than certain we'll lose the physical work at the first date. I'd feel more in control if we had one affordable family plan instead of a grand event hanging over the account. I want my sixtieth birthday to have guests, not a repayment schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Mara didn't want the extra cooking at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the home meal wouldn't be agreed just because I'd found a cheaper line on the budget. I'd share the preparation and clearing, or we'd discuss another affordable plan before inviting anyone. I wouldn't save money by quietly handing my partner a second shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the birthday saving establish an affordable retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an unbooked hall isn't cash we already own, and a smaller party doesn't replace a wage. We'd still need actual income dates, amounts and costs before choosing whether to stop. A future celebration and a future job both need more than a hopeful sentence from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives me room to learn today's job better without pretending I know the last day I'll work. I'd be 68 in 2036 and about 71 when the capable robots followed. I'd still enjoy trying a useful function now, not write myself off because the later number looks old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My actual worry over the next few years would still be a smaller paid week or a winter bill with so little saved. The physical jobs look less immediately exposed than planning, but low wages and few local firms don't disappear because full AGI is distant. I don't know whether I'd have a suitable offer or the ability for a physical job at 69, or what confirmed retirement resources we'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pack leftovers twice weekly, checking whether food spending actually fell by the hoped-for 8 after costs, and keep the current paid repair work with the usual electrical checks and daily checked AI explanations. I'd request available free evening community advice now on actual resources and review the household records yearly with Mara, sooner if either wage fell. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Mara's agreement. We'd count no unknown pension payment, automatic help from grown children or promised future work capacity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our small present margin, and less hurried by the distant technology date. I'd still look forward to a neat repair or a Sunday lunch. Worrying about rent doesn't mean I've stopped enjoying the ordinary week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children be part of the later household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there were actual offers they wanted and could afford to make, with the details agreed. I wouldn't assume wages, accommodation or care from the fact that we brought them up. I want my children at Sunday lunch because they're family, not because the budget needs another earner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the future figures showed neither affordable exit nor suitable paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd take the actual shortfall to available advice and check what real help or options existed then. I'd count only work I could actually do and an employer actually offered. A longer warning doesn't create a future body, job or payment that hasn't been confirmed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because planning changes could reduce my paid week first and I expect heavy repair-hour losses when robots follow around 2031, with Mara's laundry work exposed too. Clear paid hours, affordable ways to test practical work and checked household resource figures would help. I'd like my next plan to have a price and a person agreeing to pay, not just my name at the top.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether using AI every day means I know more about retirement than somebody who won't touch it. I can get a tidy paragraph out of a program and still need somebody to check an actual eligibility date. Being quick with a new button doesn't put another month's rent in the account.

headlineQuote: Being quick with a new button doesn't put another month's rent in the account.
portrait: Karl, **58**, is an experienced mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary wiring and repairs.
He has **lower pay**, eighteen days saved, few similar employers and rent, with laundry-press partner Mara and grown children living elsewhere.
His **daily AI explanations** don't inspect wiring; new voice notes require approved access, free paid practice, maintained wages and original-measurement checks.
His **private repair idea** depends on permission, coverage, affordable costs and actual demand, while retirement resources and later ability remain unknown.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected heavy repair-hour loss around 2031, with earlier paid-time pressure and possible losses in Mara's laundry wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid hours**, affordable practical trials and checked household resource figures would turn plans into costed choices rather than assumed income.
